extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal scholars, and practitioners of English constitutional and parliamentary law
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the constitutional rules governing parliamentary procedure (royal assent, publication, adjournment/prorogation, dissolution) and the doctrines of the royal title and succession (hereditary nature, mode of descent, limitations by Parliament, immediate vesting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal assent: methods, forms, and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The royal assent may be given in person (the king comes to the house of peers, the titles of bills read, and the clerk declares the king's answer in Norman-French) or by letters patent under the great seal (statute 33 Hen. VIII. c. 21). When the bill has received the royal assent in either of these ways, it is then, and not before, a statute or act of parliament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-person formulae: for a public bill the clerk declares 'le roy le veut' ('the king wills it so to be'); for a private bill 'soit fait come il est desire' ('be it as it is desired'); on refusal 'le roy s'avisera' ('the king will advise upon it'). Assent by letters patent must be signed and notified to both houses assembled together in the high house. Only after royal assent in either form does a bill become law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute publication and promulgation
rubrics_metrics.description: An act of parliament, thus made, is placed among the records of the kingdom and needs no formal promulgation to give it the force of law, because every man in England is, in judgment of law, party to the making of an act of parliament by his representatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although formal promulgation is unnecessary, a copy is usually printed at the king's press for public information. Historically (before printing) the king's writ sent transcripts to the sheriff of every county commanding that 'ut statuta illa... publice proclamari, et firmiter teneri et observari faciat' — statutes were to be publicly proclaimed at county courts and kept for reading/copying (usage continued until Henry VII).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts bind all subjects including the king; royal dispensation unlawful
rubrics_metrics.description: An act of parliament is the exercise of the highest authority and hath power to bind every subject in the land, and the dominions thereunto belonging; nay, even the king himself, if particularly named therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The act cannot be altered, amended, dispensed with, suspended, or repealed but in the same forms and by the same authority of parliament. It was formerly held that the king might in many cases dispense with penal statutes, but statute 1 W. & M. st. 2. c. 2 declares that suspending or dispensing with laws by regal authority, without consent of parliament, is illegal. Maxim: it requires the same strength to dissolve as to create an obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjournment (house-level) and prorogation (parliament-level): definitions and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: An adjournment is a continuance of the session from one day to another effected by the authority of each house separately; the adjournment of one house is no adjournment of the other. A prorogation is the continuance of the parliament from one session to another effected by royal authority and both houses are necessarily prorogued at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjournment preserves the state of business so proceedings may continue without fresh commencement. Prorogation puts an end to the session: bills only begun and not perfected must be resumed de novo (if at all) in a subsequent session. Historically, prorogation was sometimes used after the king gave assent at end of session; statute 1 Car. I. c. 7 and later provisos addressed whether royal assent determined session. The modern rule is that a prorogation must be expressly made to determine a session.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prorogation mechanics and royal power to recall in emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Prorogation is effected by royal authority, expressed either by the lord chancellor in his majesty's presence, by commission from the crown, or frequently by proclamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If at the time of an actual rebellion, or imminent danger of invasion, the parliament shall be separated by adjournment or prorogation, the king is empowered (statute 30 Geo. II. c. 25) to call them together by proclamation, with fourteen days notice of the time appointed for their reassembling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution of parliament: three modes and constitutional rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: A dissolution is the civil death of the parliament and may be effected three ways: (1) by the king's will (royal prerogative), (2) by the demise (death) of the crown, and (3) by expiry of the permitted duration (statutory term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) By the king's will: the crown has the prerogative to prorogue or put a final period to parliament; this prevents parliament becoming perpetual. 2) Demise of the crown formerly dissolved parliament immediately; statutes (7 & 8 W. III. c. 15 and 6 Ann. c. 7) now provide that the parliament in being shall continue for six months after the death of any king or queen unless sooner prorogued or dissolved by the successor, and provide for assembly where separated. 3) By time: statute 6 W. & M. c. 2 allowed three years' maximum; statute 1 Geo. I. st. 2. c. 38 prolonged it to seven years — as constitution now stands parliament must expire at the end of every seventh year if not sooner dissolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme executive invested in a single person; immediate investiture
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme executive power of these kingdoms is vested by our laws in a single person, the king or queen; the person entitled to it, whether male or female, is immediately invested with all the ensigns, rights, and prerogatives of sovereign power (statute 1 Mar. st. 3. c. 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sex makes no difference to investiture; upon entitlement the sovereign receives full executive rights. This principle underpins doctrines of succession and continuity of government explored in the chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental doctrine of succession: four cardinal propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitutional maxim is: (1) the crown is, by common law and constitutional custom, hereditary; (2) hereditary in a manner peculiar to itself; (3) the right of inheritance may from time to time be changed or limited by act of parliament; (4) when so limited, the crown remains hereditary in the new proprietor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter proposes to prove these four branches by historical examples, doctrines of ancient lawyers, and statutes which from time to time create, declare, confirm, limit, or bar hereditary title to the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary nature of the crown and rationale against elective monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: The crown is in general hereditary, descendible to the next heir on the death or demise of the last proprietor; the English monarchy has been hereditary rather than elective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone argues elective monarchy, while theoretically preferable, tends to produce influence, partiality, artifice, and civil strife in practice; hereditary succession was chosen to avoid periodic bloodshed and instability (with historical examples such as Rome, Poland, Germany). The hereditary title is not jure divino in English law but arises from founders of the constitution and immemorial usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular mode of inheritance (peculiarities from feudal descent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of inheritance generally corresponds with the feudal course of descent but with material exceptions: males preferred to females and primogeniture among males observed; on failure of male line the crown descends to the issue female; among females the eldest daughter alone (and her issue) succeeds, not all daughters jointly; doctrine of representation applies; on failure of lineal descendants the crown goes to collateral relations provided they descend from the blood royal; succession of half-blood relatives is allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Edward V succeeded in preference to his elder sister Elizabeth; Mary I succeeded to Edward VI; the line of Margaret queen of Scots succeeded on failure of Henry VIII's male line. Representation and proximity rules illustrated by cases (e.g., Richard II, Henry IV). The rationale for eldest daughter sole: necessity of sole succession to the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary right is defeasible by Parliament (not indefeasible)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of hereditary right does not imply an indefeasible right to the throne — the supreme legislative authority (king and both houses of parliament) may defeat this hereditary right by particular entails, limitations, and provisions and vest inheritance in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory and parliamentary language 'the king's majesty, his heirs, and successors' indicates that while 'heirs' implies a general hereditary right, 'successors' implies that this inheritance may sometimes be broken through. Practical necessity: Parliament must have power to set aside an unsuitable heir (lunatic, idiot, incapable) for the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate vesting of the crown in the successor; continuity ('the king never dies')
rubrics_metrics.description: However the crown may be limited or transferred, it remains descendible and becomes hereditary in the wearer of it; immediately upon the natural death of one sovereign the right of the crown vests eo instanti upon his heir — 'the king is said never to die' in his political capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms: haeres natus (heir by descent) or haeres factus (heir made by settlement). There can be no interregnum; the right of sovereignty is invested in the successor by descent. Analogy to landed estates: once transferred, the property is hereditary in the new owner unless limited by conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest transfers the crown subject to existing laws and inheritability
rubrics_metrics.description: When the crown is transferred by conquest (e.g., William the Conqueror), the inherent properties of the crown (notably descendibility) transfer with it: the conqueror acquires the right to possess the crown but must take it subject to the existing laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone explains that conquest gave title to possess the crown, not to change the nature of government; the new possession becomes a new estate of inheritance and the conqueror's family transmits the crown as hereditary thereafter, subject to the nation's laws.
